questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes Breadth‑First Search (BFS) from Depth‑First Search (DFS) with respect to completeness, optimality (for unit step cost), time complexity, and space complexity?

options.A: BFS is complete and optimal (for unit step cost) with time O(b^{d+1}) and space O(b^{d+1}); DFS is also complete and optimal, with the same time and space bounds.
options.B: BFS is complete but not optimal; DFS is complete and optimal, both with exponential time and space.
options.C: BFS is complete and optimal (for unit step cost) with exponential time and space; DFS may fail to be complete and is not optimal, with exponential time but only linear space.
options.D: Both BFS and DFS require only linear space in the worst case.

questions.question: Under which condition does Breadth‑First Search guarantee an optimal solution?

options.A: BFS always returns an optimal solution, regardless of step costs.
options.B: BFS returns an optimal solution only when every action has the same cost.
options.C: DFS returns an optimal solution only when every action has the same cost.
options.D: Neither BFS nor DFS can guarantee optimality when step costs vary.

questions.question: Consider a problem where the shallowest goal appears at depth d and the maximum tree depth is m ( m > d). Which uninformed search algorithm expands fewer nodes in the worst case?

options.A: BFS expands fewer nodes because it stops as soon as depth d is reached.
options.B: DFS expands fewer nodes because it goes straight down to depth m before backtracking.
options.C: Both BFS and DFS expand the same number of nodes in the worst case.
options.D: Neither algorithm expands any nodes if the goal is at depth d.

questions.question: Which statement accurately captures the trade‑off between BFS and DFS regarding memory consumption?

options.A: BFS requires O(b^{d+1}) memory, while DFS needs only O(b · m) memory, where m is the maximum depth explored.
options.B: Both BFS and DFS need O(b^{d+1}) memory because they store all generated nodes.
options.C: BFS needs only linear memory, whereas DFS needs exponential memory.
options.D: Memory usage for both algorithms is independent of the branching factor b.

options.A: It eliminates the need for any observed evidence during inference.
options.B: It allows the joint distribution to be factorized into a product of local CPTs, facilitating efficient computation of posterior probabilities.
options.C: It guarantees that all variables are independent of each other.

questions.question: Which of the following statements most accurately defines rule‑based reasoning and provides an appropriate example of its use?

options.A: It is a deductive process that generates new sentences by applying inference rules; e.g., using Modus Ponens on the Horn clauses C ∧ (B ⇒ A) to infer A.

options.D: It is a heuristic search that explores state spaces without formal inference; e.g., hill‑climbing on a SAT problem.

questions.question: Which scenario best illustrates forward chaining in a rule‑based deduction system?

questions.question: Why are first‑order representations considered essential for achieving strong generalization in knowledge representation?
